claim: Cell size homeostasis is a property that is conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: Maintenance of cell size homeostasis is a property that is conserved throughout eukaryotes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about cell size homeostasis across eukaryotes.

claim: Cell size homeostasis is brought about by the co-ordination of cell division with cell growth.
source: Cell size homeostasis is brought about by the co-ordination of cell division with cell growth and requires restriction of smaller cells from undergoing mitosis and cell division, whilst allowing larger cells to do so.
evidence: This statement draws from established understanding of cell size control mechanisms.

claim: Cell size homeostasis requires restriction of smaller cells from undergoing mitosis and cell division, whilst allowing larger cells to do so.
source: Cell size homeostasis is brought about by the co-ordination of cell division with cell growth and requires restriction of smaller cells from undergoing mitosis and cell division, whilst allowing larger cells to do so.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of how cell size homeostasis operates, based on established knowledge.

claim: Cyclin-CDK is the fundamental driver of mitosis.
source: Cyclin-CDK is the fundamental driver of mitosis and therefore ultimately ensures size homeostasis.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the role of cyclin-CDK in cell cycle control.

claim: Cyclin-CDK ultimately ensures size homeostasis.
source: Cyclin-CDK is the fundamental driver of mitosis and therefore ultimately ensures size homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of cyclin-CDK in driving mitosis and the requirement for mitosis control in size homeostasis.

claim: Inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK encodes cell size information.
source: We develop a high-throughput single-cell assay system of CDK activity in vivo and show that inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK encodes cell size information, with the phosphatase PP2A aiding to set a size threshold for division.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the high-throughput single-cell assay system described in the manuscript.

claim: The phosphatase PP2A aids to set a size threshold for division.
source: We develop a high-throughput single-cell assay system of CDK activity in vivo and show that inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK encodes cell size information, with the phosphatase PP2A aiding to set a size threshold for division.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PP2A's role in establishing size thresholds.

claim: CDK inhibitory phosphorylation works synergistically with PP2A to prevent mitosis in smaller cells.
source: CDK inhibitory phosphorylation works synergistically with PP2A to prevent mitosis in smaller cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that the combined effects of CDK phosphorylation and PP2A exceed their individual contributions.

claim: Diploid cells of equivalent size to haploid cells exhibit lower CDK activity in response to equal cyclin-CDK enzyme concentrations.
source: Finally, we find that diploid cells of equivalent size to haploid cells exhibit lower CDK activity in response to equal cyclin-CDK enzyme concentrations, suggesting that CDK activity is reduced by increased DNA levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing haploid and diploid cells.

claim: CDK activity is reduced by increased DNA levels.
source: Finally, we find that diploid cells of equivalent size to haploid cells exhibit lower CDK activity in response to equal cyclin-CDK enzyme concentrations, suggesting that CDK activity is reduced by increased DNA levels.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that diploid cells have lower CDK activity than haploid cells of equivalent size.

claim: Scaling of cyclin-CDK levels with cell size contributes to cell size homeostasis.
source: Therefore, scaling of cyclin-CDK levels with cell size, CDK inhibitory phosphorylation, PP2A, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity, all inform the cell cycle network of cell size, thus contributing to cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between cyclin-CDK levels and cell size.

claim: CDK inhibitory phosphorylation informs the cell cycle network of cell size.
source: Therefore, scaling of cyclin-CDK levels with cell size, CDK inhibitory phosphorylation, PP2A, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity, all inform the cell cycle network of cell size, thus contributing to cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the role of tyrosine phosphorylation in size-dependent CDK regulation.

claim: PP2A informs the cell cycle network of cell size.
source: Therefore, scaling of cyclin-CDK levels with cell size, CDK inhibitory phosphorylation, PP2A, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity, all inform the cell cycle network of cell size, thus contributing to cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing PP2A's role in size-dependent CDK regulation.

claim: DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity informs the cell cycle network of cell size.
source: Therefore, scaling of cyclin-CDK levels with cell size, CDK inhibitory phosphorylation, PP2A, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity, all inform the cell cycle network of cell size, thus contributing to cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that diploid cells have lower CDK activity than haploid cells of equivalent size.

claim: Cells display homeostatic behaviour in maintaining population cell size by controlling cell size at mitosis.
source: Cells display homeostatic behaviour in maintaining population cell size by controlling cell size at mitosis (Fantes et al., 1975; Ginzberg et al., 2015; Wood and Nurse, 2015; Lloyd, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cell size homeostasis is driven by larger cells being more likely to divide than smaller cells.
source: This homeostasis is driven by larger cells being more likely to divide than smaller cells, resulting in the correction at cell division of cell size deviances (Fantes et al., 1975; Fantes, 1977; Patterson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) is the master regulator of mitosis and cell division.
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDKCdc2) is the master regulator of mitosis and cell division, and therefore the propensity for smaller cells not to divide must ultimately feed into the regulation of CDK activity (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and established knowledge about CDK's role.

claim: The propensity for smaller cells not to divide must ultimately feed into the regulation of CDK activity.
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDKCdc2) is the master regulator of mitosis and cell division, and therefore the propensity for smaller cells not to divide must ultimately feed into the regulation of CDK activity (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on CDK's role as master regulator and the observation that smaller cells divide less frequently.

claim: Cyclin synthesis and subsequent binding of cyclin to CDK drives CDK into a catalytically competent form.
source: CDK activity is subject to several mechanisms of control: cyclin synthesis and subsequent binding of cyclin to CDK, which drives CDK into a catalytically competent form Solomon et al., 1990;
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Wee1 kinase acts to inhibit CDK through regulatory tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Wee1 kinase and Cdc25 phosphatase act to inhibit or activate CDK, respectively, through regulatory tyrosine phosphorylation (Nurse, 1975; Russell and Nurse, 1986; Gould and Nurse, 1989);
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cdc25 phosphatase acts to activate CDK through regulatory tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Wee1 kinase and Cdc25 phosphatase act to inhibit or activate CDK, respectively, through regulatory tyrosine phosphorylation (Nurse, 1975; Russell and Nurse, 1986; Gould and Nurse, 1989);
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP2A phosphatase works to remove phosphates deposited by CDK reducing its net activity.
source: and PP2A phosphatase works to remove phosphates deposited by CDK reducing its net activity (Kinoshita et al., 1990; Kinoshita et al., 1993; Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2009; Mochida et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2016),
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PP2A controls the phosphorylation state of Wee1 and Cdc25 to regulate the level of CDK tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: and also controls the phosphorylation state of Wee1 and Cdc25 to regulate the level of CDK tyrosine phosphorylation (Lucena et al., 2017; Hutter et al., 2017; Rata et al., 2018; Kamenz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The CDK control network co-ordinates cell division with cell growth through an unknown mechanism that responds to cell ploidy.
source: Finally, the CDK control network also co-ordinates cell division with cell growth through an unknown mechanism that responds to cell ploidy, with cell size generally doubling as ploidy doubles (Wood and Nurse, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation and acknowledges an unknown mechanism.

claim: Cell size generally doubles as ploidy doubles.
source: Finally, the CDK control network also co-ordinates cell division with cell growth through an unknown mechanism that responds to cell ploidy, with cell size generally doubling as ploidy doubles (Wood and Nurse, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Potential size control pathways will be integrated at the level of CDK activity control because CDK activity is the driver of mitosis.
source: It is likely that potential size control pathways will be integrated at the level of CDK activity control because CDK activity is the driver of mitosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on CDK's role as the driver of mitosis.

claim: In fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, it has been proposed that size control was mediated by the DYRK kinase Pom1.
source: For example, in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, it has been proposed that size control was mediated by the DYRK kinase Pom1, which ultimately inhibits mitotic onset by causing the inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK by signalling through the Wee1 kinase (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Pom1 ultimately inhibits mitotic onset by causing the inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK by signalling through the Wee1 kinase.
source: For example, in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, it has been proposed that size control was mediated by the DYRK kinase Pom1, which ultimately inhibits mitotic onset by causing the inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation of CDK by signalling through the Wee1 kinase (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In both the absence of Pom1 itself or the absence of inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation, cells are able to maintain cell size homeostasis.
source: However, in both the absence of Pom1 itself or the absence of inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation, cells are able to maintain cell size homeostasis (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010; Wood and Nurse, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There must exist alternative mechanisms by which fission yeast cells integrate cell size information into the CDK control network.
source: Thus, there must exist alternative mechanisms by which fission yeast cells integrate cell size information into the CDK control network.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cells maintain size homeostasis even without Pom1 or tyrosine phosphorylation.

claim: Much of our understanding of cyclin-CDK network regulation has been derived from in vitro studies.
source: Much of our understanding of cyclin-CDK network regulation has been derived from in vitro studies, but these have limitations when considering cellular parameters such as cell size (Mochida et al., 2016; Pomerening et al., 2005; Pomerening et al., 2003; Sha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: In vitro studies have limitations when considering cellular parameters such as cell size.
source: Much of our understanding of cyclin-CDK network regulation has been derived from in vitro studies, but these have limitations when considering cellular parameters such as cell size (Mochida et al., 2016; Pomerening et al., 2005; Pomerening et al., 2003; Sha et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of in vitro studies, supported by citations.

claim: The C-CDK fusion-protein is expressed under the Cyclin BCdc13 promoter.
source: This C-CDK fusion-protein is expressed under the Cyclin BCdc13 promoter, and therefore C-CDK expression mimics endogenous Cyclin B expression.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental system used in the study.

claim: C-CDK expression mimics endogenous Cyclin B expression.
source: This C-CDK fusion-protein is expressed under the Cyclin BCdc13 promoter, and therefore C-CDK expression mimics endogenous Cyclin B expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the use of the Cyclin B promoter.

claim: C-CDKAF strains are healthy and viable.
source: These C-CDKAF strains are healthy and viable, but have markedly distinct cell cycle profiles from C-CDKWT expressing strains, as they spend a significantly longer period in G1 than C-CDKWT cells (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation and observation.

claim: C-CDKAF strains have markedly distinct cell cycle profiles from C-CDKWT expressing strains.
source: These C-CDKAF strains are healthy and viable, but have markedly distinct cell cycle profiles from C-CDKWT expressing strains, as they spend a significantly longer period in G1 than C-CDKWT cells (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: C-CDKAF cells spend a significantly longer period in G1 than C-CDKWT cells.
source: These C-CDKAF strains are healthy and viable, but have markedly distinct cell cycle profiles from C-CDKWT expressing strains, as they spend a significantly longer period in G1 than C-CDKWT cells (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: C-CDKAF cells co-ordinate cell division with cell growth and maintain cell size homeostasis.
source: Nevertheless, C-CDKAF cells co-ordinate cell division with cell growth and maintain cell size homeostasis (Figure 1a; Wood and Nurse, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: C-CDKWT and C-CDKAF show clear oscillations with degradation of C-CDK occurring just before cell division.
source: This analysis showed clear oscillations of C-CDKWT and C-CDKAF, with degradation of C-CDK occurring just before cell division (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: C-CDKAF oscillations were more variable.
source: C-CDKAF oscillations were more variable, and 5% of the C-CDKAF cells trigger C-CDK degradation in the absence of division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar to what has been observed in CDK1AF expressing human cells (Pomerening et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 5% of the C-CDKAF cells trigger C-CDK degradation in the absence of division.
source: C-CDKAF oscillations were more variable, and 5% of the C-CDKAF cells trigger C-CDK degradation in the absence of division (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar to what has been observed in CDK1AF expressing human cells (Pomerening et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation.

claim: In both C-CDKWT and C-CDKAF backgrounds, C-CDK concentration scaled with cell size.
source: In both backgrounds, C-CDK concentration scaled with cell size, with C-CDKWT exhibiting a higher amount of C-CDK at mitotic entry compared to C-CDKAF (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: C-CDKWT exhibits a higher amount of C-CDK at mitotic entry compared to C-CDKAF.
source: In both backgrounds, C-CDK concentration scaled with cell size, with C-CDKWT exhibiting a higher amount of C-CDK at mitotic entry compared to C-CDKAF (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: For C-CDKWT both cell size and C-CDK level reach sharp thresholds at which cell division rates increase.
source: On investigating the links between the probability of a given cell to divide, cell size, and C-CDK level, we found that for C-CDKWT both cell size and C-CDK level reach sharp thresholds at which cell division rates increase (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1e.

claim: In the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation, a sharp threshold for C-CDKAF levels is present but occurs at a lower level than C-CDKWT.
source: In the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation, a sharp threshold for C-CDKAF levels still is present (Figure 1e), but occurs at a lower level than C-CDKWT.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: C-CDKAF cells fail to generate a sharp threshold for cell size.
source: C-CDKAF cells fail to generate a sharp threshold for cell size, but even without a clear size threshold, C-CDKAF cells still restrict smaller cells from division (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Even without a clear size threshold, C-CDKAF cells still restrict smaller cells from division.
source: C-CDKAF cells fail to generate a sharp threshold for cell size, but even without a clear size threshold, C-CDKAF cells still restrict smaller cells from division (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Cut3 translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus upon CDK-dependent phosphorylation of a single site in its N-terminus.
source: We used Cut3, the Smc4 homolog, as a CDK activity biosensor, because it translocates from the cytoplasm into the nucleus upon CDK-dependent phosphorylation of a single site in its N-terminus (Figure 1f; Sutani et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1f.

claim: The Cut3 nuclear/cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio can be used to assess CDK activity.
source: Thus, the Cut3 nuclear/cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio can be used to assess CDK activity, a method that has been applied to other protein kinases (Spencer et al., 2013; Araujo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research using similar methods.

claim: The response of the maximum nuclear Cut3 concentration to 1NM-PP1 was similar to the one measured in a previous phosphoproteomics study.
source: The response of the maximum nuclear Cut3 concentration to 1NM-PP1 was similar to the one measured in our previous phosphoproteomics study (Swaffer et al., 2016), confirming that the sensor reflects in vivo CDK activity (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by citation and data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The Cut3 sensor reflects in vivo CDK activity.
source: The response of the maximum nuclear Cut3 concentration to 1NM-PP1 was similar to the one measured in our previous phosphoproteomics study (Swaffer et al., 2016), confirming that the sensor reflects in vivo CDK activity (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous phosphoproteomics data and data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: CDK activity rises to a higher level in C-CDKWT cells in comparison to C-CDKAF cells.
source: Subsequently, we examined CDK activity in unperturbed cells measured by the Cut3 N/C ratio and showed that it both rises to a higher level in C-CDKWT cells in comparison to C-CDKAF cells and also that progress through mitosis in C-CDKAF cells is slower and more variable (Figure 1i, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Progress through mitosis in C-CDKAF cells is slower and more variable.
source: Subsequently, we examined CDK activity in unperturbed cells measured by the Cut3 N/C ratio and showed that it both rises to a higher level in C-CDKWT cells in comparison to C-CDKAF cells and also that progress through mitosis in C-CDKAF cells is slower and more variable (Figure 1i, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1i and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: During a G2/M block, cell size and C-CDK enzyme concentration scaled with each other in both C-CDKWT and C-CDKAF backgrounds.
source: During a G2/M block (Figure 1g), cell size and C-CDK enzyme concentration (as measured by C-CDK-YFP fluorescence intensity) scaled with each other in both backgrounds (Figure 1j,k).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1j and 1k.

claim: After release from CDK inhibition, C-CDKWT activity correlated well with both cell size and C-CDK protein level.
source: After the release from CDK inhibition, C-CDKWT activity correlated well with both cell size and C-CDK protein level (Figure 1l,n).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1l and 1n.

claim: Peak C-CDKAF activity correlated better with protein level than with cell size.
source: However, peak C-CDKAF activity correlated better with protein level than with cell size (Figure 1m,o).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1m and 1o.

claim: Peak CDK activity in both C-CDKAF and C-CDKWT was clearly size dependent.
source: Therefore, we repeated this experiment using a high-throughput assay based on imaging flow cytometry (Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 6) and observed that peak CDK activity in both C-CDKAF and C-CDKWT was clearly size dependent (Figure 1—figure supplement 5e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5e.

claim: CDK tyrosine phosphorylation helps to inform the cell division machinery of cell size.
source: Thus, CDK tyrosine phosphorylation helps to inform the cell division machinery of cell size (Figure 1d,l).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1d and 1l.

claim: In the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation, C-CDKAF cells are still able to generate a threshold C-CDK level for division and prevent small cells from division.
source: However, in the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation, C-CDKAF cells are still able to generate a threshold C-CDK level for division and prevent small cells from division (Figure 1e,o, Figure 1—figure supplement 5e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1e, 1o, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5e.

claim: In vivo CDK activity was dependent on C-CDK level and was reduced when CDK activity was inhibited using 1NM-PP1.
source: Results from this assay demonstrated that in vivo CDK activity was dependent on C-CDK level and was reduced when CDK activity was inhibited using 1NM-PP1 (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In all genetic backgrounds at the same level of C-CDK enzyme, maximum C-CDK activity increases with cell size.
source: In all genetic backgrounds at the same level of C-CDK enzyme, maximum C-CDK activity increases with cell size (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: The single-cell dose–response of CDK activity on C-CDKWT concentration background is clearly bistable.
source: The single-cell dose–response of CDK activity on C-CDKWT concentration background is clearly bistable, with cells existing in either an 'on' or an 'off' state.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis showing two distinct population distributions.

claim: The C-CDK concentration required to switch cells 'on' decreases with increasing cell size.
source: The C-CDK concentration required to switch cells 'on' decreases with increasing cell size, and the sharpness of the transition increases with size (Figure 2i,k).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2i and 2k.

claim: The sharpness of the transition to the 'on' state increases with cell size.
source: The C-CDK concentration required to switch cells 'on' decreases with increasing cell size, and the sharpness of the transition increases with size (Figure 2i,k).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2i and 2k.

claim: Bistable behaviour is heavily dependent on CDK tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: This bistable behaviour is heavily dependent on CDK tyrosine phosphorylation (Figure 2i,k,l).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2i, 2k, and 2l.

claim: Removal of PP2A allows the attainment of the 'on' state at lower cell sizes.
source: Removal of PP2A allows the attainment of the 'on' state at lower cell sizes (Figure 2i), effectively shifting the C-CDK dose–response curve towards lower sizes without altering the shape of the response (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2i and 2k.

claim: PP2A adds switch like behaviour to the C-CDK activity dose-response.
source: In addition, PP2A also adds switch like behaviour to the C-CDK activity dose-response, as bistable behaviour with C-CDKAF is not present with C-CDKAF PP2AΔ (Figure 2i dashed box, inset and Figure 2l).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2i and 2l.

claim: Maximum C-CDK activity increases with cell size in all genetic backgrounds, but plateaus at about 12–13 μm in the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: When looking across all size bins, maximum C-CDK activity increases with cell size in all genetic backgrounds, but plateaus at about 12–13 μm in the absence of tyrosine phosphorylation (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2j.

claim: Cell size is able to regulate C-CDK activity even in the absence of both tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A.
source: However, it is clear that cell size is able to regulate C-CDK activity even in the absence of both tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2i and 2j.

claim: Inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation directly results in a reduction of intrinsic CDK activity.
source: Inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation directly results in a reduction of intrinsic CDK activity (Berry and Gould, 1996),
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PP2A is able to regulate inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation by controlling the phosphorylation state of Wee1 and Cdc25.
source: PP2A is able to regulate inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation by controlling the phosphorylation state of Wee1 and Cdc25 (Lucena et al., 2017),
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PP2A can directly oppose the phosphorylation of CDK substrates.
source: and in addition can directly oppose the phosphorylation of CDK substrates (Godfrey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: When the contributions of tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A were added to the C-CDKAF PP2AΔ curve, they did not re-capitulate the wild-type curve.
source: However, when the contributions of tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A were added to the C-CDKAF PP2AΔ curve, they did not re-capitulate the wild-type curve (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: There is synergy between the tyrosine phosphorylation network and PP2A activity.
source: Thus, this analysis suggests that there is synergy between the tyrosine phosphorylation network and PP2A activity and that this synergy is important for establishing the C-CDK level threshold for division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that individual contributions do not sum to the wild-type behavior.

claim: Synergy between tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A is important for establishing the C-CDK level threshold for division.
source: Thus, this analysis suggests that there is synergy between the tyrosine phosphorylation network and PP2A activity and that this synergy is important for establishing the C-CDK level threshold for division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that individual contributions do not sum to the wild-type behavior.

claim: In the absence of major regulators, small cells are still able to restrict division by lowering CDK activity as a result of some other factor related to cell size.
source: Strikingly however, in the absence of these major regulators, small cells are still able to restrict division by lowering CDK activity as a result of some other factor related to cell size (Figure 2h,i,j).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2h, 2i, and 2j.

claim: Diploid cells exhibited lower C-CDK activity in response to the same C-CDK enzyme concentration as haploids.
source: Strikingly, diploid cells exhibited lower C-CDK activity in response to the same C-CDK enzyme concentration as haploids (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The EC50 of the diploid dose–response curve was almost double that of the haploid.
source: The EC50 of the diploid dose–response curve was almost double that of the haploid (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The inhibition of C-CDK activity is most marked in smaller diploid cells.
source: Looking at single-cell, volume-resolved data, the inhibition of C-CDK activity is most marked in smaller diploid cells, with larger diploid cells having almost indistinguishable dose–response curves from their haploid equivalents (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Larger diploid cells have almost indistinguishable dose–response curves from their haploid equivalents.
source: Looking at single-cell, volume-resolved data, the inhibition of C-CDK activity is most marked in smaller diploid cells, with larger diploid cells having almost indistinguishable dose–response curves from their haploid equivalents (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The effect of cell size on CDK activation is much less marked in larger than normal haploids.
source: The effect of cell size on CDK activation is much less marked in larger than normal haploids (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Cells of different ploidies, but otherwise equivalent volume, experience variable CDK activity in response to equal C-CDK level.
source: Therefore, cells of different ploidies, but otherwise equivalent volume, experience variable CDK activity in response to equal C-CDK level.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data comparing haploid and diploid cells.

claim: Even in the absence of all major CDK regulation, DNA concentration is able to lower CDK activity and prevents division in small cells.
source: This suggests that even in the absence of all major CDK regulation, DNA concentration is able to lower CDK activity and prevents division in small cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation that diploid cells have lower CDK activity than haploid cells of equivalent size.

claim: At higher volumes, DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity disappears.
source: At higher volumes, this inhibition of CDK activity disappears, and so the regulation may operate through titrating out an inhibitor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that larger diploid cells behave similarly to haploid cells.

claim: The regulation may operate through titrating out an inhibitor.
source: At higher volumes, this inhibition of CDK activity disappears, and so the regulation may operate through titrating out an inhibitor.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the size-dependent DNA inhibition of CDK activity.

claim: CDK activity regulation through inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A work synergistically to communicate information about cell size to the CDK control network.
source: We propose that CDK activity regulation through inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation and PP2A work synergistically to communicate information about cell size to the CDK control network.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing synergy between these pathways.

claim: Cyclin-CDK complex level scales with cell size, and this aids in the prevention of division in small cells.
source: Furthermore, we show that cyclin-CDK complex level scales with cell size, and this aids in the prevention of division in small cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between cyclin-CDK levels and cell size.

claim: In cells lacking PP2A and inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation, haploid and diploid cells of equivalent size and similar cyclin-CDK concentration have differing cyclin-CDK activities, with diploid cells exhibiting a lower activity.
source: Finally, we show that in cells lacking PP2A and inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation, haploid and diploid cells of equivalent size and similar cyclin-CDK concentration have differing cyclin-CDK activities, with diploid cells exhibiting a lower activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing haploid and diploid cells.

claim: Cyclin-CDK activity is increased in cells of lower ploidy.
source: This suggests that cyclin-CDK activity is increased in cells of lower ploidy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that haploid cells have higher CDK activity than diploid cells of equivalent size.

claim: Cell size control over the onset of mitosis involves several molecular mechanisms.
source: Our observations suggest that cell size control over the onset of mitosis involves several molecular mechanisms.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the multiple mechanisms identified in the study.

claim: One mechanism of cell size control is the accumulation of cyclin through the cell cycle, which scales with the increase in cell size.
source: If it is assumed that the accumulation of the C-CDK cyclin chimera driven by the cyclin promoter mimics the accumulation of cyclin, then one mechanism is the accumulation of cyclin through the cell cycle, which scales with the increase in cell size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C-CDK levels scale with cell size.

claim: A second mechanism of cell size control is a synergistic interaction between the inhibitory CDK tyrosine phosphorylation pathway and the PP2A phosphatase.
source: A second is a synergistic interaction between the inhibitory CDK tyrosine phosphorylation pathway and the PP2A phosphatase, which acts on both the tyrosine phosphorylation pathway and dephosphorylation of CDK substrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing synergy between these pathways.

claim: The third mechanism of cell size control is a DNA-concentration-dependent inhibition of CDK activity.
source: The third is a DNA-concentration-dependent inhibition of CDK activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that diploid cells have lower CDK activity than haploid cells of equivalent size.

claim: Given the conservation of all these molecular regulators, these mechanisms can be expected to have direct relevance in other eukaryotic cells.
source: Given the conservation of all these molecular regulators, these mechanisms can be expected to have direct relevance in other eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the molecular regulators across eukaryotes.

claim: CDK activity vs C-CDK level dose–response curves previously demonstrated in vitro operate in vivo.
source: Our results demonstrate that C-CDK activity vs C-CDK level dose–response curves previously demonstrated in vitro operate in vivo, but in addition, we show that they are dependent on cell size in vivo (Pomerening et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous in vitro work.

claim: CDK activity vs C-CDK level dose–response curves are dependent on cell size in vivo.
source: Our results demonstrate that C-CDK activity vs C-CDK level dose–response curves previously demonstrated in vitro operate in vivo, but in addition, we show that they are dependent on cell size in vivo (Pomerening et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing size-dependent dose-response curves.

claim: CDK activity can be inhibited by a DNA-related mechanism in keeping with early work showing that increasing DNA content delays mitosis.
source: We propose that CDK activity can be inhibited by a DNA-related mechanism in keeping with early work showing that increasing DNA content delays mitosis, with the removal of DNA by irradiation causing acceleration of the following mitosis (Devi et al., 1968; Sachsenmaier et al., 1970; Wilson, 1925).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by current experimental data and citations to early work.

claim: DNA inhibits CDK activity more in smaller cells, potentially reducing CDK activity by a titration mechanism.
source: Our experiments show that DNA inhibits CDK activity more in smaller cells, potentially reducing CDK activity by a titration mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and is a speculative mechanism.

claim: DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity may be related to the mechanism by which cell size is linked to ploidy across cell types.
source: This may be related to the mechanism by which cell size is linked to ploidy across cell types (Wilson, 1925; Amodeo and Skotheim, 2016; Prescott, 1956; Tzur et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative connection supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation, PP2A activity, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity act together to restrict small cells from division.
source: Finally, we show that tyrosine phosphorylation, PP2A activity, and DNA-dependent inhibition of CDK activity act together to restrict small cells from division, forming a mechanism to generate the robust cell size threshold behaviour observed in normal cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data showing the combined effects of these mechanisms.

claim: Both PP2A+ and PP2AΔ cells arrest in an almost uniform G2 state following endogenous CDK1 inactivation after temperature shift.
source: Following endogenous CDK1 inactivation after temperature shift, both PP2A+ and PP2AΔ cells arrest in an almost uniform G2 state, ensuring that downstream analysis is not confounded by cells arresting in different phases of the cell cycle (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: C-CDK levels increased similarly upon induction in all mutant backgrounds.
source: C-CDK levels increased similarly upon induction in all mutant backgrounds (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Population mean C-CDK activity was comparable between all conditions.
source: Population mean C-CDK activity was comparable between all conditions (Figure 2h);
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: C-CDK activity displayed differences at the single-cell level when activity was measured in cells of different sizes.
source: however, C-CDK activity displayed differences at the single-cell level when activity was measured in cells of different sizes.
evidence: This is supported by single-cell data analysis.
